messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Anong, a 76-year-old mechanic with hands as skilled and steady as they were fifty years ago, first came to the clinic after her husband found her frozen in the middle of their garage, staring at the open bay door with an expression of pure terror. For six months, a man from her neighbourhood had stalked her. It began with him waiting at the end of her street as she walked home from the bus stop, then escalated to him following her to the grocery store. The ordeal culminated one evening when she was tending her small vegetable garden; she looked up to see his face pressed against her kitchen window, watching her. He was arrested, but for Anong, he never truly left. The police report closed the case, but her own sense of dread remained wide open, a constant, humming alarm inside her.

The terror now lives in the most ordinary moments. The smell of rich, damp soil—a scent she once associated with the satisfaction of a well-tended garden—has become a potent trigger. Working on a customer's truck last week, the earthy smell from the mud-caked tires was enough to plunge her back into that evening. The memory doesn’t arrive as a story, but as a series of stark, silent photographs flashing in her mind: the imprint of his shoe in the soft dirt by her roses, the pale oval of his face in the darkening glass of the window, the way his eyes were fixed on her. These images are so vivid and immediate that the grease on her hands and the metal of the wrench she holds seem to fade away, replaced by the feeling of cold dread and the certainty that she is being watched.

These photographic intrusions instantly ignite a profound sense of threat. The moment the memory-image of his face appears, her body floods with adrenaline. She is no longer a mechanic in her own garage; she is prey. Her senses sharpen to an excruciating degree, and she becomes superalert, her head on a swivel. Every shadow in the corner of the garage seems to lengthen and take shape, every scrape of metal from the street outside sounds like a footstep. This feeling of being on guard follows her into her house, a place that once felt like a sanctuary. She finds herself constantly checking behind her as she walks from room to room, her heart pounding, certain she will see him. Her husband’s gentle reassurances are meaningless against the visceral conviction that danger is imminent.

This state of hypervigilance has become a feedback loop, a self-sustaining engine of fear. The more she scans her environment for threats, the more her mind seems to conjure the very memories that fuel her anxiety. Standing at the kitchen sink, her eyes darting towards the garden window, she finds the photographic image of his face there replaying on a loop. This constant state of alert also makes her far more sensitive to her triggers. The ordinary stress of a difficult repair job, or even the scent of outdoor air drifting through an open door, is now enough to send a jolt of panic through her, as her threat-primed mind interprets it as a sign of his presence. The memories have so thoroughly poisoned her world that even moments of peace feel dangerous. When she finds herself feeling relaxed or happy, sitting with her husband in the evening, a secondary wave of anxiety hits her; she has come to believe that letting her guard down is an invitation for him to return.

The cycle has left her isolated within her own experience. When her husband sees the fear on her face, he asks what’s wrong, but Anong cannot make him understand. When she tries to explain what is happening in her mind, she loses the thread of the story, the words dissolving before she can form them. The sheer distress of holding the photographic images in her mind while trying to narrate them becomes so overwhelming that she has to push them away, leaving her silent and trembling, her husband watching her with a helpless confusion that has slowly built a wall between them. She has stopped gardening entirely, and the garage, her lifelong domain of competence and control, now feels like a trap. It was after she snapped at her husband for suggesting they sit outside on a sunny afternoon that she finally made the call. She came to therapy hoping to reclaim her home, to feel the sun on her face without flinching, and to one day smell the earth after a rainstorm and feel nothing but peace.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not describe how the trauma memory itself makes the patient more sensitive to her triggers.
